source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same; price-level conditions rejected (shift test); support/resistance levels approximated by rolling swing/Donchian extremes since Grimes gives no precise level-finding algorithm

candidates.name: PotentialSupportResistanceLevel
candidates.quote: the best we can say about a support area is that it is an area where price may have a higher probability of pausing
candidates.description: Primitive: approximate a 'potential' support/resistance level as the extreme (highest high / lowest low) of the last N bars. Downstream candidates test price behavior around this level; this is a design decision, not the book's own precise algorithm, since Grimes deliberately declines to give one.
candidates.pseudocode: level = lowest(low, levelLookback) [support case]; level = highest(high, levelLookback) [resistance case]

complexity.reason: Grimes explicitly treats support/resistance as a probabilistic zone, not a rule ('always attach the qualifier potential'); the authoring pass must choose a concrete level definition (recent swing extreme, session extreme, round Donchian window, etc.)

notes: Grimes stresses S/R should be zones, not exact lines ('a crayon, not a drafting pen'); a band around the rolling extreme is left as a parameter for the authoring pass.

candidates.name: PriceRejectionFromLevel
candidates.quote: when price reaches a support area that will hold, there is an immediate (in the context of the time frame) and sharp movement away from the level
candidates.description: A sharp, immediate move away from a tested level: the bar (or next bar) closing well away from the level touch by more than a multiple of ATR -- the archetypal sign that a level holds.
candidates.pseudocode: low[1] <= level + touchMargin AND (close[0] - level) > rejectionMultiple * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: the rejection test itself is an ATR-scaled bar-range comparison once a level is given; the level input carries G04-01's research-grade design decision

notes: Grimes contrasts this with a slow trend grinding down into support (no rejection, more likely to break) -- see G04-07.

candidates.name: SpringUpthrustFakeout
candidates.quote: A spring is a quick drop below support, which immediately finds enough demand to push prices back above support
candidates.description: Wyckoff spring (long side): a quick dip below the support level that immediately recovers back above it within a bar or two. Mirrored on the top side is the upthrust: a push above resistance followed by an immediate failure back below it.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < level - marginPoints AND close[0] > level
candidates.book_order_type: market at next open once confirmed, per convention

complexity.reason: a bar-range comparison against G04-01's level

notes: Grimes's own naming: spring = bottom-side fakeout, upthrust = top-side; the mirrored sides field already captures both, so they are recorded as one candidate rather than two.

candidates.name: BrokenLevelRetestHolds
candidates.quote: support, once violated, becomes resistance
candidates.description: A level that was broken (price closed through it) is later retested from the other side and holds -- broken support acting as new resistance (mirrored: broken resistance acting as new support).
candidates.pseudocode: anyOf(k in 1..breakLookback, close[k] < level) AND high[0] >= level - retestMargin AND close[0] < level

complexity.reason: needs to track a level across time from break to retest, on top of G04-01's design decision

candidates.name: CleanLevelBreakFollowThrough
candidates.quote: Clean levels actually tend to set up good breakout trades beyond the level
candidates.description: A level that has shown 1-3 clean price-rejections (G04-02) and is then decisively closed through -- expect strong breakout follow-through; bias entries in the breakout direction rather than fading.
candidates.pseudocode: cleanRejectionCount(level, testLookback) >= 1 AND cleanRejectionCount(level, testLookback) <= 3 AND close[0] beyond level by breakMargin*atr(atrLength)
candidates.book_order_type: market at next open once broken, per convention

complexity.reason: needs a persistent count of clean-rejection touches against G04-01's level

candidates.name: MultipleTestsWeakensLevel
candidates.quote: If price is able to return to the level three or more times, probabilities begin to shift in favor of the level breaking
candidates.description: A level that has been touched three or more times within a lookback window is more likely to fail than hold -- bias entries toward an eventual break rather than continuing to fade the level.
candidates.pseudocode: touchCount(level, touchLookback, touchMargin) >= 3

complexity.reason: a persistent touch counter against G04-01's level

notes: Grimes explicitly rejects the traditional view that more tests strengthen a level: 'this is one of those pieces of the conventional wisdom that is absolutely wrong.'

candidates.name: NoRejectionAtLevelPrecedesFailure
candidates.quote: Price quickly found itself back up against the level, and consolidated there for many bars ... This is not what we should see if a level is going to hold
candidates.description: Price consolidates in a narrow range right at a level (small bar ranges, little movement away) rather than showing G04-02's price rejection -- precedes the level failing; bias toward a break rather than a bounce.
candidates.pseudocode: countIf((high[k]-low[k]) < tightMultiple*average(high-low, rangeLookback) AND abs(close[k]-level) < nearLevelMargin, consolidateBars) >= consolidateBars - allowedMisses

complexity.reason: a persistent multi-bar narrow-range-near-level counter, on top of G04-01's level

candidates.name: StopBeyondSupportExtreme
candidates.quote: Stop B is probably the most logical stop, a tick beyond the most extreme level reached in the support area
candidates.description: Protective stop placed a small offset beyond the most extreme price reached within the tested support (resistance) area -- Grimes's 'Stop B', chosen for respecting the pattern's geometry.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] <= lowest(low, rangeLookback)[1] - stopBuffer
candidates.book_order_type: stop beyond the range extreme (mechanized as close-and-next-open)

complexity.reason: a window low/high plus a fixed buffer

notes: Essentially StopBeyondRecentRangeExtreme; recorded because it is Grimes's own worked example ('Stop B') with a named rationale, distinct from the 'Stop A' variant below (G04-09) and the wider, more-random 'Stop C'.

candidates.name: StopInsideLevelEarlyExit
candidates.quote: The stop marked A, actually inside the support level ... has the benefit of virtually eliminating slippage even in thin markets because you are exiting long before the mass of other stop orders is hit
candidates.description: A conservative stop placed a fraction of the way from the entry price toward the support/resistance extreme (inside the zone itself, not beyond it) -- exits ahead of the crowd's stop cluster at the level extreme, trading a higher chance of premature stop-out for less slippage.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] <= entryPrice - stopInsideFraction*(entryPrice - level)
candidates.book_order_type: stop inside the level (mechanized as close-and-next-open)

complexity.reason: a fraction-of-distance comparison

candidates.name: TradingRangeRandomWalkContext
candidates.quote: Because markets in trading ranges tend to approximate random walks, most traders are well advised to avoid trading within the randomness of these structures and to limit any involvement to the margins
candidates.description: Primitive/context filter: identify a 'trading range' state -- price contained within a band for N bars without net directional progress -- and suppress mid-range entries, restricting entries to the margins (support/resistance tests).
candidates.pseudocode: (highest(high,rangeLookback) - lowest(low,rangeLookback)) < rangeAtrMultiple*atr(atrLength) AND abs(close[0]-close[rangeLookback]) < netMoveAtrMultiple*atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: 'trading range' is a design decision about how much net directional progress and containment counts as 'ranging'; the pseudocode is one reasonable proxy, not Grimes's own algorithm

candidates.name: RangeExpansionNotBreakout
candidates.quote: Drop below range just expands the range. Support is now lower ... Many times, the range is simply expanded
candidates.description: A close beyond the established range boundary that, within M bars, settles back into a new (shifted) but still-bounded range rather than trending away -- treat as range expansion, not a true breakout; do not read the boundary break alone as a trend signal.
candidates.pseudocode: close[k] beyond old range boundary for some k in last expandLookback bars AND (highest(high,reboundBars) - lowest(low,reboundBars)) < rangeAtrMultiple*atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: needs to track the old range boundary through the break and re-test containment afterward

candidates.name: DiagonalSlopingRangeComplexPullback
candidates.quote: the diagonal range sloping against the higher time frame trend ... could be considered the most common pullback pattern
candidates.description: A parallel trading range whose slope runs counter to the higher-timeframe trend is, functionally, a complex pullback (G03-17) playing out on the trading timeframe. Springs near support (or upthrusts near resistance) within it are especially strong with-trend entries (see G04-21).
candidates.pseudocode: G04-10 (bounded range) AND rangeSlope opposes htfTrendDirection

complexity.reason: combines range detection with a slope-of-range measure and a higher-timeframe direction read

notes: Cross-chapter composite: reuses Chapter 3's complex-pullback definition (G03-17) rather than redefining it.

candidates.name: TightConsolidationAgainstRangeEdgePrecedesBreak
candidates.quote: a tighter consolidation against resistance often leads to a break of that resistance ... this is more indicative of pressure building against that side of the range
candidates.description: Price consolidates in a narrow band pressed against one edge of a larger range (small bar ranges clustered near the range's upper or lower boundary) -- a precursor to a breakout in that direction, rather than the price-rejection pattern expected of a level that will hold.
candidates.pseudocode: countIf((high[k]-low[k]) < tightMultiple*average(high-low, rangeLookback) AND close[k] within nearEdgeFraction*(rangeHigh-rangeLow) of rangeHigh, consolidateBars) >= consolidateBars - allowedMisses

complexity.reason: combines a rolling range boundary, a positioning-within-range test, and a persistent narrow-bar counter

notes: Also the basis for the classic 'cup and handle' pattern per Grimes; not separately recorded since it reduces to this same test.

candidates.name: ConvergingRangeVolatilityCompression
candidates.quote: the market making successively smaller swings, as if zeroing in on a target price level. The edges of this range appear to converge
candidates.description: The average bar range over a recent window is smaller than the average bar range over the window preceding it -- volatility compression (a symmetrical/converging triangle), sets up a breakout-mode filter.
candidates.pseudocode: average(high-low, recentWindow) < contractionMultiple*average(high-low, priorWindow)

complexity.reason: two trailing window averages compared

candidates.name: DoNotFadeFirstBreakoutFromConvergence
candidates.quote: My trading rules for triangles are simple and reduce to one principle: do not fade the first breakout from one of these formations
candidates.description: After G04-14 (volatility compression) fires, block countertrend/fade entries on the first close beyond the compressed range's boundary; only with-breakout entries are allowed.
candidates.pseudocode: G04-14 fired within compressLookback bars AND proposedEntry direction == breakout direction

complexity.reason: a persistent bars-since flag on G04-14 plus a direction check

candidates.name: AscendingTriangleHigherLowsIntoResistance
candidates.quote: price holds successively smaller declines (higher lows) into a clearly defined resistance level ... typically shows strengthening conviction on the part of buyers ... usually leading to a breakout above that resistance
candidates.description: A series of successively higher swing lows forms against a flat resistance level -- strengthening buyer conviction, biasing toward an eventual upside breakout (mirrored: successively lower swing highs into flat support, a descending triangle).
candidates.pseudocode: swingLow[0] > swingLow[1] AND swingLow[1] > swingLow[2] AND abs(swingHighLevel - resistanceLevel) < levelTolerance

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and a flat-level test on the opposite side

candidates.name: ExpandingRangeVolatilityAvoidEntries
candidates.quote: widening triangles where each swing, both up and down, is bigger than the preceding swings ... I avoid these types of environments or at least significantly reduce risk in them
candidates.description: Each with-trend and countertrend swing is larger than the swing preceding it, in both directions (an expanding range) -- volatility is growing unpredictably; block new entries or reduce size.
candidates.pseudocode: swingLength[0] > swingLength[1] AND swingLength[1] > swingLength[2] AND signAlternates(swing[0], swing[1], swing[2])

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection with alternating-direction and growing-amplitude tests

candidates.name: SpikeReverseSpikeTriangleWarning
candidates.quote: Whenever a market makes a very large, sharp movement in one direction, followed by a similar move in the other direction ... the normal expectation ... is for the market to spend a period of time consolidating
candidates.description: A very large-range bar (or short run of bars) in one direction quickly followed by a similar-sized move in the opposite direction predicts a period of directionless, triangle-like consolidation -- block new entries for N bars after this pattern.
candidates.pseudocode: ((high[k1]-low[k1]) > rangeMultiple*average(high-low,rangeLookback) AND close[k1] > open[k1]) AND ((high[k2]-low[k2]) > rangeMultiple*average(high-low,rangeLookback) AND close[k2] < open[k2]) for k1, k2 within spikePairLookback of each other

complexity.reason: reuses a large-range-bar test (as G03-04) paired in opposite directions within a lookback

candidates.name: ContinuationRangeHigherTimeframeCheck
candidates.quote: the higher time frame will often tell a simple story: the trading time frame trend may have pushed the higher time frame into an overbought or overextended condition, and the unreadable range on the trading time frame is actually just a simple pullback on the higher time frame
candidates.description: An otherwise-unreadable trading-timeframe range is treated as a continuation (pullback) pattern when the higher-timeframe proxy (G03-35, a much longer moving-average slope) still agrees with the prior trend direction.
candidates.pseudocode: G04-10 (bounded range) AND htfTrendDirection (G03-35 test) == priorTrendDirection

complexity.reason: inherits G03-35's higher-timeframe design decision

candidates.name: ReversalRangeHigherTimeframeOverextension
candidates.quote: Any of the factors that can suggest an end of a trend on one time frame (overextension, momentum divergence, specific terminating formations, etc.) apply to all time frames
candidates.description: A trading-timeframe range is treated as a potential higher-timeframe reversal (rather than continuation) when the higher-timeframe proxy shows overextension (G03-11, distance from EMA in ATR units, evaluated on a longer lookback) or a momentum divergence (G03-13).
candidates.pseudocode: G04-10 (bounded range) AND (G03-11 evaluated at htfLookback OR G03-13 evaluated at htfLookback)

complexity.reason: compounds two Chapter 3 research/moderate-grade primitives at an approximated higher-timeframe lookback

candidates.name: SpringNearSupportInLargerUptrendEntry
candidates.quote: Be on guard for springs near support in larger-scale uptrends, and for upthrusts near the highs of these patterns in downtrends. These offer exceptional entries into higher time frame trends
candidates.description: A spring (G04-03) occurring near the support edge of a diagonal, higher-timeframe-trend-aligned range (G04-12) -- an especially strong with-trend entry.
candidates.book_order_type: market at next open once confirmed, per convention

complexity.reason: inherits G04-12's higher-timeframe and range-slope design decisions

rejected.quote: the levels in these examples are random price levels!
rejected.reason: a meta-validity caution about how believable random lines look, not itself a bar-level trading condition

rejected.quote: Take a price chart of any market and hide the bars. ... Draw random lines on the chart.
rejected.reason: a self-experiment exercise for the trader, not a trading rule

rejected.quote: you will discover that your win ratio is a little over 9 percent, leaving an expected value of zero
rejected.reason: illustrative random-walk expected-value math, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: I have not found volume to be important and have found my trading signals to be as reliable as those generated by traders who focus on volume
rejected.reason: methodological opinion on the (non-)importance of volume, not itself a testable bar-level condition

rejected.quote: many traders will size positions based on the risk in the trade
rejected.reason: position sizing, not a bar-level rule

rejected.quote: if holding overnight, these levels are prone to large overnight gap risk, and, furthermore, these tend to be opening gaps that do not reverse
rejected.reason: a risk caution, not phrased as a mechanical bar-level condition

rejected.quote: Expect additional volatility and slippage. Your risk is probably at least twice what you think it is.
rejected.reason: execution/slippage commentary, not a bar-level condition

chapter_summary: Chapter 4 treats support/resistance as probabilistic zones rather than lines, works through the spring/upthrust fake-out, price rejection as the tell for a level holding vs. failing, three named stop-placement choices around a tested level (Stop A inside, B beyond the extreme, C further out), and the trading-range taxonomy: parallel box (with range-expansion-not-breakout), diagonal/sloping range as a complex pullback, tight consolidation against one edge, converging/triangle volatility compression with a do-not-fade-the-breakout rule, the ascending-triangle bias, and expanding/widening ranges to avoid. Several candidates deliberately depend on Chapter 3 primitives rather than redefining them: G04-12 and G04-19/20 reuse G03-17 (complex pullback), G03-35 (higher-timeframe alignment), and G03-11/G03-13 (EMA-distance overextension, momentum divergence) at a longer, higher-timeframe lookback.
